analysis.one_liner: Closes a loophole letting employer health plans cap mental health visits, not just dollars.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee after being referred to three House committees and two subcommittees; it never received a vote or a hearing in the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1996 federal mental health parity law stopped employer health plans from setting lower total dollar caps on mental health benefits than on medical and surgical benefits, but plans could still limit how many therapy visits a patient could use each year. This bill would have closed that gap by extending the parity rule to limits on the number of visits or other non-dollar benefit limits. It was referred to three House committees in July 1999 and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with employer-sponsored health insurance who need mental health care. Under the 1996 parity law, a plan could obey the letter of the law by matching dollar caps while still cutting off coverage after, say, 20 therapy visits a year — a limit far easier to hit than a dollar cap. Closing that loophole would have meant more covered visits for people treating depression, anxiety, and other mental health conditions, with the protection applying to plan years beginning on or after July 1, 2000 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with employer health plans needing mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Extends the federal mental health parity rule beyond dollar caps: the 1996 law only required plans to set equal annual and lifetime dollar limits on mental health benefits; this bill amends ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, and the Internal Revenue Code so the same equal-treatment rule covers limits on the number of visits or other non-dollar benefit limits [S2][S3].

The change would take effect for group health plan years beginning on or after July 1, 2000, with a delayed effective date for plans governed by collective bargaining agreements already in force [S3].
It also updates the HIPAA regulatory transition provision so regulations written for the parity rules cover the expanded scope [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor or self-insure group health plans would bear the cost of covering more mental health visits, which would show up as higher premiums or reduced plan flexibility. Plans could no longer contain mental health costs through visit caps while matching medical dollar caps on paper.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers offering group plans

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a benefit mandate on employers and insurers during a period when group plans were already managing costs; covering more mental health visits would raise premiums or plan costs, and the bill contains no funding or offset to cushion that [S3].

The bill is narrow: it polices the form of limits (visit counts versus dollar counts) but leaves plans free to impose higher copayments, deductibles, or prior-authorization requirements on mental health care, so parity in practice would still be incomplete [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it closes a specific escape hatch in the 1996 parity law — using visit caps instead of dollar caps — for workers with employer coverage. The cost falls on insurers and employers through richer mental health benefits. The bill's weakness is that it is a patch, not a overhaul: cost-sharing differences and utilization-review hurdles would remain, so plans would have other ways to constrain mental health coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees when introduced in July 1999, then parked in two subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on July 1, 1999, joined by 11 original cosponsors, most from New York [S1][S3].

The Speaker referred it to three committees with jurisdiction over health benefits — Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — a split referral that makes passage harder because the bill must satisfy multiple committees [S5].

In July and August 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations; no further action of any kind appears in the record, and no version was ever reported out of committee or debated [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001 without a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to cap mental health visits even while complying with the 1996 dollar-cap parity rule. People with employer coverage who need mental health care gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers, who keep visit caps

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew recorded votes, so no roll-call split exists; its 12 cosponsors were 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, mostly from New York.

industries.note: Insurers used visit caps as a cost-control tool on mental health benefits; the bill would have barred that method, forcing them to structure mental health coverage like medical coverage. Their gain from the bill dying was keeping that tool.

Employers, including self-insured plans governed by ERISA, would face higher benefit costs if mental health visit limits had to match medical coverage. Some workers bargain for these benefits, so the cost and the benefit both land inside the employment relationship.
Therapists, psychiatrists, and clinics would see more covered visits and fewer patients cut off mid-treatment by visit caps.
